newsitem.title: USA: Vail Resorts moves higher in heavy trading.
newsitem.headline: Vail Resorts moves higher in heavy trading.

text.p: An avalanche of demand drove shares of Vail Resorts Inc up over 10 percent at the Wall Street debut of the toney ski resort on Tuesday.

Shares rose 2-1/4 to 24-1/4 in early trading after company officials rang the opening bell to signal the start of trading at the New York Stock Exchange. Within an hour, over three million shares had traded hands.
The stock was in high demand because of its strong brand name, its rank as one of the leading players in the skiing industry and the prospect of consolidation in the industry, analysts said.

Vail, headquartered in Avon, Colo., is the largest and most popular ski mountain complex in North America with 1.65 million skier days in the 1995-1996 winter season, according to the company's prospectus. The company operates Vail as well as Beaver Creek, Keystone and Breckenridge in Colorado.

"Vail is very good at bringing in the destination skier," said Kevin Eldridge, analyst at Vancouver, British Columbia-based Salman Partners. "Destination skiers" refers to skiers who visit a resort usually for several days and tend to be more affluent than local day skiers.
He also cited Vail's plan to reach for revenues beyond the winter season by turning the resort into a four season resort. Vail offers golfing, tennis, horseback riding, and other activities.

The resort has also branched into real estate as part of its strategy. While sales of ski lift tickets have grown each year over the past 10 years, Vail said revenue from other sources has grown at a much faster rate, accounting for 41 percent of resort revenues in fiscal 1996.

However, its aggressive acquisition strategy in Colorado has raised eyebrows at the U.S. Department of Justice. Vail has agreed to sell its Arapahoe Basin operations by June 2 to settle antitrust concerns. Arapahoe is the highest ski area in North America, with a summit elevation of 13,050 feet.

According to its prospectus, Vail Resorts Inc has a nine percent share of skier days in the United States, nearly 40 percent greater than that of its nearest competitor. "Skier days" means the total number of days spent by individual skiers on mountains.
The number two ski resort in the United States behind Vail, as defined by skier days, is Breckenridge, also owned by Vail.
Shares in the IPO priced at $22 each, above the estimated pricing range of $19 to $21 each, according to lead underwriter Bear Stearns & Co Inc.
Other underwriters of the deal are Furman Selz, Goldman Sachs & Co, Salomon Brothers Inc, Schroder Wertheim & Co and Smith Barney Inc.

Selling shareholders offered 7.1 million shares in the IPO, up from an original estimate of 5.5 million shares, bringing the total number of shares to be offered to the public to 12.1 million. Vail sold five million shares.
